# GROUNDTRUTH: MASTER BUILD PLAN — CALIFORNIA SELF-SERVE LEGAL SOFTWARE (PAID, PROOF-FIRST, SUBSCRIPTION)

This document supersedes GROUNDTRUTH_CA_MVP_BUILD_PLAN.md and GROUNDTRUTH_RETENTION_M... [title cut off in source PDF]. It is the single source of truth. All prior decisions from our working sessions are incorporated.

*Transcribed verbatim (to the extent OCR/page-image reading allows) from a 22-page PDF upload, `01813d4a-GROUNDTRUTH_MASTER_BUILD_PLAN.pdf`, footer-credited "Generated by Kimi." No edits made to content or intent; any illegible or cut-off text in the source is marked `[...]` below rather than guessed at.*

## MISSION

Launch a paid, California-only self-help legal document product that is visibly different from LegalZoom because it shows its proof — and structurally different because its documents never expire. A visitor finds a document, completes the interview free, sees every clause beside its source, quote, check date and honest verification level, then pays to download a document stamped with a public, privacy-safe verification page. Subscribers' documents stay current: when the law changes, they are told and can update in one click. Every claim shown to users must be generated from real data and be literally true.

Positioning sentence for all copy: "Documents that never expire."

Go-to-market wedge: California single-member LLC formation first. All other launch-set documents ship quietly behind it.

Business model: per-document one-time purchase plus a subscription (monitoring, updates, credits, signing) — the Microsoft model: this is software, not a legal service. Law changes are the software updates; the subscription keeps everything current.

Scope lock: California only. Pure self-serve software — no lawyers, no attorney referral, no e-filing, no filing on behalf of users, no registered agent service (referral link only). Owner has decided: no attorney review and no E&O insurance at launch — accepted risk, logged in DECISIONS.md. The design-level UPL controls in Part 10 are NOT optional; they carry the load.

## CURRENT STATE (from the full system map — already built, do not rebuild)

- 741 CA documents, 6,621 clauses, 11,688 citations; three honest verification levels; A/B/C tiers computed from clause verification.
- Citation-recheck pipeline (CourtListener + direct fetches) with triage workflow and CI gate.
- Free tier fully client-side: search/browse, interview wizard with conditional clauses, live preview with inline sourcing, text/PDF/DOCX parity-tested exports, contract reader, filing next-steps with computed SoI deadline and calendar reminder.
- Trust layer: /verify/ pages, export footer IDs, /trust page, methodology page, copy-linter build gate.
- Paid: per-document Stripe test-mode checkout, server-side release-document paywall, RLS on entitlement tables (adversarially retested), portal sessions, admin refunds via shared secret.
- Sharing & signing: share-view/share-sign with typed/drawn signature and sealed PDF certificate (disclosed as not a certified e-signature service).
- Account & library: local-first document library with optional per-document cloud sync, version history with corpus drift detection, purchase history, delete-account, list-sessions.
- Ops: send-review-requests (once per entitlement), error/feedback ingestion, structured analytics (no third-party tracker), shared rate limiter.
- CI: 47 test files, 7-job pipeline, static build via tools/build_site.py, GitHub Pages deploy, merge-guard.
- Deliberately not built: registered-agent filing service, e-filing, admin-role login system, QR codes anywhere, and — the whole point — no legal advice.

## GLOBAL RULES

1. Inform, never advise. No copy may recommend a legal course of action, assess the strength of a user's position, or claim legal sufficiency, enforceability, or outcomes.
2. Never file anything on behalf of a user. The product informs and instructs only; the user files.
3. Free and in-browser with no account: search, marketed document pages, the interview, the live preview, all sourcing badges, quotes, check dates, verification levels, the filing instruction sheets, and the contract reader. Paid export and cloud features may require the backend. (Browse-all is retired — see Part 8.)
4. Never mark a clause Verified or change a checkedDate without re-verifying it against a primary source. Record sourceClass on every citation: primary-official, court-opinion, agency, mirror, secondary. A mirror is not primary.
5. Before every commit run `python validate_corpus.py`, `node regression.js`, `python merge_guard.py`, and any newer gates. Do not commit on failure.
6. Never touch config.js contents or commit secrets.
7. Never auto-edit legal clause text from verifier output. Write patch files, show me the diff, wait for approval.
8. Never run destructive or irreversible actions (DROP, DELETE, force-push, deploy, publish, live-mode Stripe, real charges) without showing the exact action and waiting for my yes.
9. Never store card data. Store only Stripe ids. Build and test in Stripe test mode only.
10. All paywall enforcement is server-side. Client-side gating is cosmetic only.
11. Correctness beats breadth: unverifiable content is labeled or removed from the launch set, never shipped as Verified.
12. Agent work goes on child branches or worktrees and is handed over for review. Do not commit directly to the main working branch.
13. Every number or claim on a public page is generated from the corpus or verifier output, never typed by hand.
14. Referral and partner links must carry a plain disclosure line and must never leak user data (no field values, names, or identifiers in URLs or query params).
15. Ambiguity: choose the most conservative option, log it in DECISIONS.md, continue.
16. After each step update BUILD_STATUS truthfully and report: step id, files changed, checks and results, skipped items and why, next step. Keep reports short.
17. Recommendations and lifecycle suggestions are generated ONLY from the human-reviewed relation map (Part 4) and from dates/events the user explicitly entered. Never from an AI assessment of the user's situation, never from scraped behavior profiles. If no reviewed relation exists, show nothing.
18. Recommendation and suggestion copy is factual and reviewed: "commonly used alongside," "next in this filing path," "documents related to hiring." Never "you need," "protect yourself," "avoid liability," or any phrasing the copy linter flags.
19. Tone personalization applies ONLY to pre-authored clause variants stored in the corpus and run through the same verification pipeline as every other clause. Never runtime-generate or AI-rewrite legal text. Authority clauses (those making legal claims) never vary by tone.
20. Templates store field values, clause selections, and tone settings only — never edited legal text. Legal text always renders from the live corpus, so drift detection and verify pages stay truthful for template-generated documents.
21. Retention features use no dark patterns: no fake urgency, no countdown timers, one-click unsubscribe everywhere, deleting account deletes drafts/templates/preferences.
22. No field values, names, or user content in analytics events or server logs.
23. New tables (relations, drafts metadata, templates, preferences, suggestion events) get RLS scoped to auth.uid() with adversarial tests, same standard as entitlements.

## PART 1: MAKE THE TRUST CLAIM TRUE

### STEP 1: Baseline (no code changes)

Re-measure from scratch: documents, clauses, citations, tier counts, verifier coverage, open findings by severity, unverified clauses, and clauses relying on mirror or secondary sources. Write MVP_BASELINE.md and flag any mismatch with BUILD_STATUS.

### STEP 2: Honest labels and tiers

1. Replace the single "Verified" meaning with three visible levels on every clause: Cited (citation, quote, check date), Verified (primary-source check passed), Adversarially checked (survived the verifier with no open findings). The sourcing badge shows level, check date, and a one-line plain explanation.
2. Add sourceClass to all citations, backfilled by URL domain. List every mirror or secondary clause in verifier/NON_PRIMARY_SOURCES.md, starting with the 9 small-claims CCP sections, and queue them for primary-source re-verification.
3. Redefine tiers. Tier A requires at least one authority clause, all authority clauses adversarially checked with zero open findings, a golden fixture per branch, fresh check dates, and an accessibility pass. Documents with no authority clauses get the label "Drafting only (no legal authority claimed)" and are never Tier A.
4. Update methodology.html, tiering.py, validate_corpus.py, the picker, and the sourcing UI. Recompute tiers.
5. Acceptance: no clause or document shows a level it has not earned.

### STEP 3: Corpus schema future-proofing (California-only content)

1. Add a `state` field (default "CA") to documents, clauses, citations, and filing-instruction data. All launch content is "CA"; no other state content is created.
2. Add the field to validate_corpus.py so every record carries it.
3. Purpose: expansion later must be a data load, not a schema migration.
4. Acceptance: validation fails on any record missing `state`.

### STEP 4: Mechanical controls

1. Add a pre-commit and pre-push hook plus a CI check that blocks agent-session commits to the main working branch.
2. Add a CI check that fails any change to legal text lacking an approved patch id in the commit message.
3. Acceptance: a deliberately violating test commit is blocked.

### STEP 5: Define the launch set (owner decision: propose, then WAIT)

1. Propose 100 to 150 documents with reasoning, weighted to the most common California business and individual needs: LLC and corporation formation, operating agreement, offer letter, independent contractor agreement, handbook items, NDA, residential lease, demand letter, will, advance health care directive, small claims, name change, and similar.
2. Inside the proposal, mark the wedge cluster: the single-member LLC formation path (formation documents, operating agreement, Statement of Information reminder, filing instructions, registered agent referral) that Wave 1 marketing points at.
3. WAIT for my approval. Only launch-set documents are published, promoted, and sold. Others stay in the app but are not featured, indexed, or purchasable.

### STEP 6: Verify the launch set

1. Estimate cost and time for the adversarial verifier on every authority clause in the launch set, plus checks on drafting clauses for advisory language, internal contradiction, and jurisdiction disclosure. WAIT for approval, then run in parallel batches with a resume file.
2. Triage blockers, then majors, then all minors in the launch set. For each blocker and major, show the clause, evidence, and patch. Apply only after my approval, re-verify against the primary source, update checkedDate, add a changelog.html entry.
3. Re-verify from primary sources: the 9 small-claims CCP sections, the small-claims judgment-enforcement clause, and the name-change SB 59 / AB 1084 clause.
4. Resolve the AI Transparency Act item (§ 22757.2 and SB 1000 changes) from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. If unreachable, add exact URLs and questions to OWNER_TODO.md and keep those clauses unverified.
5. Anything unconfirmable is labeled unverified and the document is excluded or clearly labeled.
6. Produce verifier/LAUNCH_SET_REPORT.md: finding rates by category, severity, and failure type.
7. Acceptance: zero open blockers or majors in the launch set; every launch-set authority clause has a recorded result.

## PART 2: PAYMENTS AND SERVER-SIDE DELIVERY

### STEP 7: Pricing decision (owner decision: propose, then WAIT)

1. Write PRICING_OPTIONS.md comparing (a) per-document one-time purchase, (b) subscription with unlimited documents, (c) hybrid: per-document purchase plus a subscription delivering the Part 9 value stack (monitoring, one-click updates, monthly document credit, unlimited edits/re-exports, unlimited e-signature).
2. For each, list exactly what is paywalled (final PDF, .docx, plain text, JSON, sources appendix, cloud save, e-signature, sharing) and what stays free. Propose defaults for edits and re-exports included in a purchase.
3. Include a 30-day money-back guarantee in every option as a marketed feature, with the exact refund-policy copy flagged for owner approval.
4. Recommend one with reasoning (default recommendation: hybrid). Leave price points as placeholders in config/pricing.json for me to fill in. WAIT for my decision.

### STEP 8: Entitlements and server-side release

1. Use Supabase migrations (not manual SQL) to confirm or extend `orders` and `order_items`, and add `entitlements` (user_id, type, document_id nullable, source order or subscription id, status, starts_at, ends_at). RLS scoped to auth.uid(), with adversarial tests for every table (a second user cannot select, insert, update or delete). Run get_advisors after each migration.
2. Edge function release-document: verifies session and entitlement, renders the final PDF and .docx server-side from the same clause set and template as the client, returns a signed short-lived download URL. Log to audit_log: document id, corpus version, clause ids and check dates, timestamp, output hash. Never log field values.
3. Server output must pass golden text-parity tests against the client preview.
4. Guest checkout with email only (magic link); the purchase is claimed on first sign-in.
5. Remove or watermark client-side print, JSON, and text paths for paid documents.
6. Acceptance: no entitlement returns a clear "purchase required" response; entitlement returns the file; a manual client-bypass checklist is run and recorded.

### STEP 9: Stripe (test mode only)

1. Stripe Checkout through an edge function, with products and prices generated from config/pricing.json.
2. Webhooks with signature verification and idempotency (event ids stored, replays are no-ops). Handle checkout.session.completed, invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed, customer.subscription.updated and deleted, charge.refunded, charge.dispute.created.
3. Refunds: the approved 30-day money-back guarantee, an admin refund action, automatic entitlement revocation. Disputes flag the account and revoke entitlement pending review.
4. Customer portal for subscription management, receipts, and payment methods. Receipts, order history, and invoice export in the account area.
5. If any subscription exists, implement California automatic renewal requirements: clear and conspicuous terms before purchase, affirmative consent, an acknowledgment email, and cancellation as easy as sign-up. Read the statute from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, cite it in DECISIONS.md, and keep the renewal copy strictly factual (copy lint enforced).
6. Evaluate Stripe Tax. Record sales-tax treatment of digital products as a question for my accountant in DECISIONS.md. Do not assert tax conclusions.
7. Abuse controls: rate limits on checkout and release endpoints, per-entitlement download limits, anomaly alerts.
8. Acceptance: test-mode end-to-end tests pass for purchase, failed payment, refund, subscription renewal and cancellation, duplicate webhook replay, dispute, and unauthorized release.

## PART 3: DIFFERENTIATORS (WHAT MAKES THIS NOT LEGALZOOM)

### STEP 10: Show-your-work document view

1. Redesign the preview so the live document sits beside a sources panel. Selecting a clause shows its source, quote, sourceClass, check date, verification level, and known gaps. On phones, use an expandable inline layout.
2. Add an optional plain-language "why this clause is here" line per clause, written without advice and checked by the copy lint. Where missing, show nothing rather than inventing it.
3. Acceptance: every launch-set clause renders correctly in both layouts; accessibility checks pass.

### STEP 11: Verification stamp and public verify page

1. On every paid export (PDF and .docx), add a short document ID and a footer line: "Sources and check dates for this document: [URL]". (No QR codes — the product deliberately has none.)
2. Create /verify/ showing: document title, generated-on date, corpus version, every clause id with its level and check date, and a status line: "No clause used in this document has changed since it was generated" or the list of changed clauses with the diff. Facts only; never say whether the user must act.
3. Store only: id, document id, corpus version hash, clause ids with check dates, timestamp, output hash. No field values, names, or user input. Use unguessable ids and rate limiting. Add an adversarial test proving the page and its API expose no user data and cannot be enumerated.
4. Acceptance: the stamp appears on every export; the page works for a fresh document and for one whose clause later changed; the privacy test passes.

### STEP 12: Filing instruction sheets

1. For every launch-set document that gets filed (LLC and corporation formation, name change, small claims), generate a "how to file" sheet: filing office or portal URL, current fee, accepted payment methods, county variations where relevant, expected processing time, and what the filer receives back.
2. Every fee, address, URL, and timeline is corpus data with its own citation, sourceClass, and check date, verified the same way as clauses. Never hand-typed. Primary source is the California Secretary of State, the courts, or the county; a mirror is not primary.
3. Copy lint: instructions, never advice. "The Secretary of State charges $X" is allowed; "you should file here" is not.
4. The sheet is viewable free in the preview and ships as an appendix inside the paid export.
5. A CI check fails the build if any fee or URL in a sheet lacks a corpus source and current check date.
6. Acceptance: every sheet item carries source + check date; the sheet renders in preview and export; no advisory wording.

### STEP 13: Free contract reader as the front door

1. Make Read-a-contract reachable without an account from the home page and relevant SEO pages. Output stays "law this passage resembles" with sources and check dates, shows "no close match found" below threshold, and never assesses the contract.
2. Add a clear note on what the tool does and does not do. Run the copy lint over all wording.
3. Re-run the 55-case evaluation; no regression from 78% top-1 and 98% top-3.
4. Pasted text must not be sent to any server unless I approve in writing.
5. Acceptance: usable on mobile; accessibility passes.

### STEP 14: Law-change alerts on saved documents

1. Connect the existing drift detection to email via an edge function, for users who opted in. The email lists the changed clause and links to the diff. Facts only.
2. This is a core subscription benefit (see Part 9 for the free/subscriber split). Check all copy against California automatic renewal requirements before shipping.
3. Acceptance: a seeded clause change produces exactly one email to the right users and none to others; unsubscribe works.

### STEP 15: Statement of Information reminder (LLC/corporation purchases)

1. At purchase of formation documents, offer an opt-in reminder for the California Statement of Information. Collect only: entity type, formation date, and the reminder email. No other entity data. Sensitive-field storage follows the existing encryption option.
2. Compute the due window from entity type and formation date. Verify the computation rule against sos.ca.gov and record it in the corpus with a citation and check date.
3. Edge function sends one reminder about 60 days before the due date and one about 14 days before. Content is facts only: what the Statement of Information is, where it is filed (official sos.ca.gov link), and the current fee with its check date. Never "you must file" framing beyond stating the legal requirement with its citation.
4. Acceptance: seeded due dates produce exactly the right emails at the right offsets; unsubscribe works; no data beyond the three collected fields is stored.

### STEP 16: Referral link (registered agent only)

1. Create config/partners.json with a placeholder entry: registered_agent (name, url, price_text). Links render only when configured; placeholders ship as owner TODOs.
2. Registered agent: show the referral link at checkout for formation documents and in the post-purchase email, with the partner's price as configured text. Disclosure line required: "We may earn a commission if you use this service. We do not provide registered agent services and do not handle your legal mail."
3. No attorney referral feature: owner decision — this is a pure self-serve software product with no lawyer involvement of any kind. Do not build attorney referral links.
4. No user data may appear in partner URLs or query params (Global Rule 14). Add a test asserting this.
5. All disclosure wording goes through the copy lint.

2. A CI check fails the build if page text and data disagree.

### STEP 19: Paid experience and home page

## PART 4: RELATION MAP (THE DATA FOUNDATION FOR ALL RECOMMENDATIONS)

### STEP 20: Build document_relations in the corpus

1. Add a document_relations data file (corpus-side, versioned like the rest of the corpus) with records: from_document_id, to_document_id, relation_type, reason (one factual line), reviewed_by, reviewed_date.
2. Relation types: next_in_path (e.g., Articles of Organization → Operating Agreement → Statement of Information), commonly_paired (e.g., Independent Contractor Agreement + NDA), lifecycle (e.g., hiring → Offer Letter, Handbook items), variant_of (e.g., single-member vs multi-member operating agreement).
3. reason strings are written by the agent, then run through the copy linter, then flagged reviewed only after owner approval. CI gate: any relation without reviewed_by + reviewed_date does not render anywhere.
4. Start with the 7-document wedge cluster fully mapped, then the rest of the 128-document launch set. Propose the wedge map first and WAIT for owner approval before marking reviewed.
5. Acceptance: validate_corpus.py checks referential integrity (both document ids exist, no self-loops, no duplicates); CI fails on unreviewed relations in rendered output.

### STEP 21: Recommendation surfaces

1. Post-purchase screen: up to 3 "documents commonly used alongside this one" cards, from reviewed relations only, each with its reason line and the target document's tier and verification summary.
2. Document page sidebar: "related documents" strip, same source.
3. Dashboard (Step 28): "suggested for you" section combining relations with the user's saved/purchased documents — deterministic set difference, computed client-side where possible.
4. Empty state: if no reviewed relations exist for a document, the surface renders nothing. No filler.
5. Acceptance: every rendered suggestion traces to a reviewed relation record; copy lint passes on all reason lines; surfaces pass accessibility.

## PART 5: TONE PERSONALIZATION

### STEP 22: Tone system design (owner decision: propose, then WAIT)

1. Write TONE_OPTIONS.md proposing launch tone levels (recommend two, named as style registers: "plain" and "formal" — never "light/strong," "soft/aggressive," or anything implying legal strength), which clause families they apply to (drafting clauses only — e.g., payment terms wording, reminder/demand phrasing), and 3 before/after examples.
2. State explicitly in the doc and in UI copy: tone changes wording style, not legal content; authority clauses are identical across tones.
3. WAIT for owner decision on levels and examples.

### STEP 23: Clause variants in the corpus

1. Extend the clause schema: a clause may have `variants` keyed by tone, each variant a full pre-authored text with its own id. Default (no tone chosen) = the base text.
2. Variants flow through the existing pipeline exactly like clauses: verifier runs per variant, golden fixtures per variant, merge-guard tracks per variant, tier computation is per-variant. A document is Tier A only if every variant of every clause passes the same standard.
3. Tone must never change an authority clause; schema enforces this (authority clauses have no variants field; validate_corpus.py fails if one appears).
4. Acceptance: golden byte-parity tests pass for each tone across the launch set; a deliberately added unverified variant fails CI.

### STEP 24: Tone UI and saved preference

1. Tone selector in the interview (one control, plain labels, short factual description of each level). Live preview updates from the selected variants — same rendering engine, parity-tested.
2. Every tone surface — selector, preference screen, export, marketing — carries the fixed line: "Tone changes wording style only. It does not change legal meaning or strength." This string is lint-protected against modification.
3. Tone preference saves to the user profile (local-first; cloud sync if signed in) and pre-fills on the next document. Per-document override always available.
4. Exports record the tone and variant ids; the verify page lists the exact variant ids used so a stamped document still lines up against sources 1:1.
5. Acceptance: changing tone re-renders preview and export identically (parity test); verify page shows variant ids; preference persists and syncs; accessibility pass.

## PART 7: RETENTION HUB AND LIFECYCLE ENGINE

### STEP 28: Dashboard (the reason to come back)

1. A returning-user home at /dashboard showing, in order: your documents (purchased, with verify links and drift status), drafts in progress, templates, upcoming dates (from Step 29), and suggested documents (from Step 21).
2. Works with no account from local data; signing in merges cloud-synced items (existing library merge pattern).
3. Every number and status on the dashboard is generated from the corpus/verifier output or the user's own records — nothing hand-typed (Global Rule 13).
4. Acceptance: dashboard renders all five sections from seeded data; empty states are honest; accessibility and performance budgets pass.

### STEP 29: Lifecycle engine (predictive intelligence, deterministic)

1. Event store: dates and events the user explicitly entered (formation date, hiring plans answered in an interview, purchase dates). No inferred behavior, no ML. Stored with the user's other data; RLS; deletable.
2. Rule table in the corpus: event → milestone → related documents/dates, all built on the reviewed relation map and on sourced deadlines (the existing SoI computation is the model to copy: rule verified against the primary source, citation + check date recorded).
3. Outputs: (a) "upcoming dates" on the dashboard (e.g., the Statement of Information window), (b) "next in your path" document suggestions at milestones (e.g., after formation: operating agreement; when a user answers that they're hiring: offer letter, contractor agreement, NDA — each with its factual reason line), (c) one opt-in email digest (monthly max) listing upcoming dates and milestone suggestions. Facts only; copy lint on every string.
4. The digest is opt-in at a clear checkbox, one-click unsubscribe, no urgency framing.
5. Acceptance: a seeded formation date produces the correct milestone list and exactly one digest per month; every suggested document traces to a reviewed relation; every date traces to a sourced rule; unsubscribe honored.

### STEP 30: Analytics for retention (extends existing structured events)

1. New events: dashboard_viewed, suggestion_shown, suggestion_clicked, suggestion_purchased, template_saved, template_used, draft_returned (opened a draft >24h after creating it), tone_changed, digest_opened, update_available_shown, update_applied.
2. No field values or user content in any event (Global Rule 22). All events behind existing analytics opt-out.
3. Internal report additions: draft return rate, template reuse rate, suggestion click-through and purchase conversion, digest engagement, update-application rate — the retention metrics this MVP exists to move.
4. Acceptance: events fire end-to-end in staging; report generates from seeded data.

## PART 8: CATALOG ACCESS MODEL (ANTI-KNOCKOFF) AND STICKINESS LOOPS

Design decision (owner-approved): no public browse-all catalog. The document list is not the product's moat — the verified corpus and pipeline are — but hiding the catalog raises copying cost and doubles as the retention mechanic: the catalog reveals itself through use. Trade-off accepted consciously: less public catalog means less public SEO surface; Wave 1 SEO pages stay public because they are the marketing.

### STEP 31: Search-first catalog (retires browse-all)

1. Replace any full-catalog browsing UI with a search-first interface: "describe what you're doing" (e.g., "I'm hiring a contractor") returns at most the top few matching documents with plain descriptions. Existing plain-language search already does this; the change is removing the enumerate-everything path.
2. Publicly browsable and indexable: only actively marketed launch-set documents (Wave 1 wedge first, per the SEO plan). All other documents: noindex, excluded from the sitemap, reachable only via a search hit or direct link.
3. No page, endpoint, or API may return a full or bulk document listing. Search responses are capped and rate-limited (extend the existing shared rate limiter). CI test: asserting the sitemap and any public route contain only marketed documents.
4. The corpus data files themselves stay out of the deployed static bundle except per-document payloads fetched one at a time.
5. Acceptance: no route or API enumerates the catalog; sitemap/CI checks pass; search still finds any launch-set document from a plain-language query.

### STEP 32: Progressive catalog reveal

1. The primary way a user discovers more documents is the reviewed relation map (Steps 20–21): post-purchase screen, library, and dashboard show "next documents in your path" for documents the user owns or has saved. Nothing else about the wider catalog is revealed.
2. Empty state rule unchanged: no reviewed relation, nothing renders.
3. Acceptance: owning document A surfaces exactly its reviewed relations; a user who owns nothing sees no catalog beyond search results and marketed pages.

### STEP 33: Unfinished-draft pull-back

1. Opt-in email sequence for saved-but-unfinished drafts: one reminder at 48 hours ("your [document title] draft is waiting"), one final reminder at 7 days, then stop permanently for that draft.
2. Facts only — document title and completion state, no urgency framing. Honors unsubscribe and the global email cap (Step 34).
3. Acceptance: seeded idle draft produces exactly two emails at the right offsets; none if finished, purchased, or unsubscribed.

### STEP 34: Post-purchase sequence and the global email cap

1. Orchestrate all lifecycle email into one scheduler with a hard cap: never more than 1 email per user per week across every sequence — receipt (immediate, transactional, exempt), day-2 template nudge ("save your answers as a reusable template" where applicable), day-7 review request (existing), idle-draft reminders (Step 33), monthly lifecycle digest (Step 29), law-change alerts (Step 14 — event-driven, exempt from the cap but batched daily).
2. One email preference center controlling every non-transactional stream; one-click unsubscribe everywhere (Global Rule 21, no dark patterns).
3. Acceptance: a seeded user eligible for every stream receives at most 1 email in any 7-day window; preference center changes take effect immediately; unsubscribe kills all non-transactional mail.

### STEP 35: Stored-value profile (switching cost without lock-in)

1. Extend the preferences profile (Step 27): a "what pre-fills now" panel showing exactly which saved fields, tone, and templates will speed up the next document. The selling point is their own data working for them, stated factually.
2. No lock-in tricks: data export stays one click and account deletion stays total (existing delete-account coverage extends to everything new).
3. Acceptance: panel reflects real saved data; export and deletion tests pass.

---

## PART 9: SUBSCRIPTION VALUE STACK (WHY SOMEONE PAYS MONTHLY)

A subscription only works if it delivers recurring value (monitoring), recurring savings (credits), or recurring utility (signing). Renting back already-purchased features does not. The subscription is three things plus the central mechanic (Step 39), each already mostly built.

### STEP 36: Monitoring bundle (the core recurring value)

1. Law-change watch on every saved document: drift detection (existing) triggers an alert email with the changed clause and diff. Free users get alerts for purchased documents only; subscribers get alerts for everything saved, including drafts and template-generated documents.
2. Deadline calendar: every date the user has triggered (Statement of Information from Step 15, plus any sourced deadline already in filing instruction sheets) appears on the dashboard with email reminders. All dates from sourced rules only (Step 29 rules apply).
3. Annual "what changed" report: one generated email/page per subscriber per year listing every corpus change that touched their saved documents. Generated from real drift data; if nothing changed, the report says so — never manufactured activity.
4. Acceptance: a seeded clause change alerts subscribers and non-subscribers per the split above; the annual report renders correctly for both a changed and an unchanged year.

### STEP 37: Economic hooks (subscribing is cheaper than not)

1. Monthly document credit: each subscription month includes one document credit, usable on any launch-set document, expiring after 12 months. Entitlement system (existing) gains a `credit` type; checkout accepts credits.
2. Unlimited edits and re-exports while subscribed; one-time purchases keep the existing edit/re-export limit. Enforced server-side in release-document (Global Rule 10).
3. Metered e-signatures: free tier gets 3 signature requests per month; subscribers get unlimited (with the existing abuse rate limits). Metering enforced server-side.
4. Partner perk: a subscriber-only discount code for the registered agent partner, if the partner offers one (config placeholder; owner obtains).
5. Acceptance: credit purchase flow works end-to-end in Stripe test mode (credit granted on renewal, consumed at checkout, expires correctly); edit/re-export and e-sign limits enforced server-side for both tiers; all limits bypass-tested.

### STEP 38: Business setup roadmap (free — this is a conversion tool, not a paywall feature)

1. A factual progress checklist on the dashboard derived from the relation map and the user's own documents: items like "Articles of Organization — done," "Operating agreement — not started," "Statement of Information — due in 47 days." Progress shown as a simple completion bar.
2. Strictly generated from owned/saved documents and reviewed relations. Copy is status only ("done / not started / due on [date]") — never "you should" framing (Global Rules 1–2, lint-enforced).
3. Free for all users, account or local — its job is to give people a reason to open the dashboard and to surface the next purchasable document.
4. Acceptance: roadmap reflects seeded document states exactly; lint passes on every string; no advisory wording.

### STEP 39: Document updates — "software updates for your documents" (the central subscription mechanic)

1. Positioning: this is a software product, not a legal service. Laws changing are the software updates. The subscription keeps every document current, the way Microsoft 365 keeps Office current.
2. When a clause in a user's saved or purchased document changes in the corpus, a subscriber gets a one-click "update this document": the document re-renders from the current corpus with the user's saved field values, clause selections, and tone preserved. The update is stored as a new version in the existing version history; the old version stays intact with its original check dates.
3. The update screen shows the diff first — what changed, the source, and the date. Facts only; never "you should update" (lint-enforced).
4. Gating: everyone sees that an update exists (the alert, Step 36 — alerts are free because they're the trust promise). Applying the update and re-exporting requires a subscription or a new one-time purchase of that document. Enforced server-side, bypass-tested.
5. Templates get the same treatment: "the underlying document changed — view the diff," with one click to rebase the template onto the current corpus.
6. Acceptance: a seeded clause change lets a subscriber update in one click with field values preserved and a clean diff shown; a free user is gated server-side; golden parity tests pass on re-rendered output; version history shows both versions with their respective check dates.

## PART 10: UPL & LEGAL-RISK SHIELD (DESIGN-LEVEL HARD GATES)

Owner decision: no attorney review, no lawyer involvement, no E&O insurance at launch — accepted risk, logged in DECISIONS.md. That makes these design controls the product's entire legal defense, and they are not optional. The legal line in California (B&P Code § 6125): mechanical document assembly from fixed templates and the user's own choices is self-help and lawful; anything individualized — recommending what fits this user's situation, assessing their position, steering their choices — is unauthorized practice of law. Every control below exists to keep the product provably on the mechanical side, and to make that provable to a court, a bar association, or a plaintiff's attorney.

### STEP 40: Advisory-language hard gates

1. Extend the copy linter into named categories, each with its own pattern set and test fixtures: (a) advice ("you should," "you need," "we recommend for your situation"), (b) outcome claims ("will protect you," "get paid," "win"), (c) enforceability/legal-strength claims ("legally stronger," "ironclad," "holds up in court"), (d) urgency/dark-pattern pressure.
2. Lint coverage extends to: all UI, all emails, SEO pages, recommendation reason lines, tone descriptions, interview question copy, dashboard strings, and marketing copy.
3. Acceptance: a deliberately violating string in each category fails the build; the linter runs in CI on every push.

### STEP 41: Tone feature reframing (highest-risk feature)

1. Tone levels use the style-register names from Step 22 (plain/formal), owner-approved.
2. The fixed line from Step 24 appears on every tone surface, lint-protected against modification.
3. No copy anywhere may compare tones by legal effect. A linter test asserts no tone description co-occurs with legal-strength vocabulary.
4. Acceptance: reframed names live everywhere; fixed line present on every tone surface; lint tests pass.

### STEP 42: Recommendation neutrality audit

1. Add an automated test proving suggestions are non-individualized: two synthetic users with identical purchased documents but different interview answers, profiles, and history must receive identical relation-based suggestions.
2. Suggestions may differ only by: documents already owned (excluded from suggestions), launch-set membership, and explicitly entered dates/events per the lifecycle rule table — each difference logged with its rule id.
3. Acceptance: the two-user test passes; a code path that personalizes suggestions from inferred behavior fails review by construction (there is no such input to the function).

### STEP 43: Interview steering ban

1. Interview questions may collect choices and explain options factually ("an arbitration clause is a clause where disputes go to arbitration; [citation]") but may never rank, recommend, or label options ("most popular," "recommended," "best for small businesses").
2. Conditional logic may show/hide options; it may not pre-select a legal option on the user's behalf. Defaults are allowed only for non-legal conveniences (formatting, dates).
3. Lint interview copy with the Step 40 categories; add a fixture test for steering language in question and help text.
4. Acceptance: linter covers interview definitions; a steering phrase in any question fails the build.

### STEP 44: Disclaimer placement

1. One canonical "what this is and isn't" notice, stored once and referenced everywhere: not a law firm, not legal advice, no attorney-client relationship, no guarantee of outcomes or enforceability, self-help tool, consult a licensed attorney for advice about your situation.
2. Rendered at: home page, interview start, checkout, every export (existing), contract reader output, dashboard, and every lifecycle/digest email footer.
3. A CI test asserts the canonical string is present in each location and is byte-identical (no drift between copies).
4. Acceptance: placement test green; owner approves final wording (Step 49).

### STEP 45: Contract reader and guarantee guardrails

1. Contract reader output is limited to "law this passage resembles" with sources and check dates; below threshold it says "no close match found." It never scores, grades, flags risk, or assesses the contract. Existing behavior — add regression tests locking it.
2. The 30-day money-back guarantee covers product quality and satisfaction only. Copy must never connect the guarantee to legal outcomes, enforceability, or filing success. Lint categories (b) and (c) apply to guarantee copy.
3. Acceptance: reader regression tests pass; guarantee copy passes lint and owner review.

### STEP 46: Legal pages and entity protections

1. Terms of Service state: the product is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice; no attorney-client relationship is formed; documents are self-help general information; the user is responsible for their own filing decisions; California jurisdiction.
2. Referral disclosures (registered agent) restate independence and the no-advice line.
3. Owner finalizes all legal pages directly (no attorney review — owner decision; accepted risk logged in DECISIONS.md).
4. Acceptance: pages drafted and owner-approved before publish.

### STEP 47: UPL incident runbook

1. Write RUNBOOK_UPL.md: on any complaint alleging unauthorized practice (bar inquiry, AG/DA contact, demand letter, journalist): preserve all records (the relation map, lint history, verifier logs, disclaimer versions are the defense — they prove mechanical operation), banner-and-hold the implicated feature if instructed, no public statements until owner decides the response, log everything in DECISIONS.md.
2. Acceptance: runbook written and linked from the ops docs.

### STEP 48: Records as the defense

1. The artifacts this plan already produces are the legal defense — keep them complete and immutable: the reviewed relation map (proves suggestions are static), copy lint history (proves advisory language was mechanically excluded), verifier logs and check dates (proves claims were sourced), disclaimer placement tests (proves notice was given), audit_log (proves what was delivered).
2. These are append-only; nothing in CI or ops may rewrite history. Retention policy documented in the data inventory.
3. Acceptance: records inventory added to the data inventory; append-only property tested for audit_log and relation map history.

### STEP 49: Accepted-risk log

1. Record in DECISIONS.md: launching without attorney review or E&O insurance is an owner-accepted risk. Keep a queued legal-questions list in OWNER_TODO.md for whenever review does happen: disclaimer strength, tone framing, subscription renewal wording, e-signature formalities for wills and health care directives (these documents have special signing rules — filing instruction sheets must state the signing requirements with sources).
2. Acceptance: the accepted risk is logged; the queued questions list exists.

### STEP 50: Copy lint extension

1. The Step 40 lint categories cover all new surfaces from Parts 4–9: emails, recommendation reason lines, dashboard strings, roadmap copy, tone descriptions, subscription marketing.
2. Acceptance: a deliberately violating string in a new surface fails the build.

### STEP 51: Tests and CI additions

1. Relation map: referential integrity, reviewed-gate enforcement, no-render-without-review test.
2. Tone: per-variant golden parity, authority-clause-no-variants schema test, verify-page variant id listing.
3. Templates: zero-legal-text scan, round-trip parity, drift notice.
4. RLS adversarial tests for: drafts metadata, templates, preferences, events, suggestion impressions.
5. Dashboard and new surfaces: accessibility (0 serious/critical) and performance budgets.
6. Catalog: no-enumeration tests (Step 31), search caps, sitemap contents.
7. Subscription: credit lifecycle, update gating, e-sign metering, email-cap enforcement.
8. Acceptance: all green in the existing 7-job pipeline; deliberately violating commits are blocked.

### STEP 53: Launch-critical product checks

1. Complete every launch-set document end to end in a real browser, desktop and phone-sized, through test-mode purchase, PDF and .docx export, filing instruction appendix, and the verify page. Fix anything broken.
2. Confirm every export includes the jurisdiction notice, the checked-dates appendix option, the filing instruction sheet where applicable, and the "what this is and isn't" notice, and makes no advice or enforceability claim.
3. Re-run accessibility (0 serious or critical) and performance budgets on the launch set.
4. Confirm analytics and feedback work end to end in staging and production config, with opt-out honored.
5. Confirm staging mirrors production, backups run, and a restore drill succeeded.
6. Add uptime and client-error alerting and a simple status page.
7. Write short incident runbooks: legal-content error (takedown, banner on affected saved documents, changelog entry), payment incident, and data incident — alongside RUNBOOK_UPL.md (Step 47).

### STEP 54: Publishable SEO pages (wedge first)

1. Re-score generated pages for unique content, citation density, and similarity.
2. Wave 1 is the single-member LLC wedge cluster only: formation documents, operating agreement, and closely related pages (about 10 to 20 pages), plus one comparison page. The comparison page shows our check dates and verification levels against a dated, manually recorded audit of what competitor pages show; the audit is stored as evidence in the repo, every claim on the page is generated from it, and the owner reviews it before publishing. Facts only; no outcome or quality claims.
3. Wave 2 is the rest of the launch set, released only after Wave 1 criteria are met.
4. Each page needs a unique title and meta description, canonical URL, schema.org markup, sitemap entry, visible check date, jurisdiction notice, price or "start free" call to action, and no advisory copy.
5. Write LAUNCH_PLAN.md: exact deploy steps, Search Console checks (indexing, thin-content signals, crawl errors), and criteria for releasing Wave 2.
6. Do NOT publish. Stop and wait for my go.

### STEP 55: User test and instrumentation

1. Write USER_TEST_PLAN.md: a script for 10 to 15 California business owners and individuals, weighted toward people forming a single-member LLC, each completing and buying one document unaided in test mode; what to observe; post-test questions including whether the sources panel, verify page, filing instruction sheet, and document-update promise changed their trust and willingness to pay; a results table; and a plain "what this is and isn't" intro.
2. Build the internal report script: per document starts, completions, completion rate, highest-abandonment step, paywall-to-checkout conversion, verify page opens, referral-link clicks (registered agent), review-request email conversions, plus the retention metrics from Step 30 and feedback categories.
3. After my go and Wave 1 live, run the report weekly and list the top 10 problems.

Write LAUNCH_READINESS.md with a pass/fail table:

## PART 13: PILOT (AFTER LAUNCH READINESS, BEFORE FULL PUSH)

### STEP 58: Pilot program

1. Cohort: 25–50 real users paying real money (Stripe live mode), weighted to the CA single-member LLC wedge. Recruit from founder/freelancer communities. Cap the cohort at what one person can support within 24 hours.
2. Duration: 4–6 weeks of active observation, plus 90-day passive retention tracking.
3. Pre-write go/no-go criteria before starting: targets for visitor→purchase on the wedge page, refund rate, interview completion rate, 60-day return rate, suggestion→purchase conversion, and update-application rate. Record them in PILOT_PLAN.md.
4. What to watch: does the sources panel / verify page / update promise move willingness to pay (the core thesis); real-world accuracy of filing instruction sheets (debrief pilot users who actually filed); registered agent referral attach rate; support load and what breaks; search quality (the hidden catalog makes search the front door — if users can't find documents by describing their need, fix this first).
5. Rule: fix bugs during the pilot; do not add features. Feature ideas go in a list for after.
6. Acceptance: PILOT_PLAN.md written with go/no-go criteria; instrumentation (Step 30 + Step 19 funnel events) verified end-to-end before the cohort starts.

## DEFERRED (not in MVP)

- E-filing or "we file it for you" service of any kind.
- Registered agent service (referral only).
- Attorney marketplace, attorney referral links, or lawyer involvement of any kind (pure self-serve software — owner decision).
- Amendment and dissolution flows, annual report filing, full compliance engine (the sourced deadline calendar in Step 36 is in scope; a full compliance product is not).
- Entity dashboard beyond the Step 28 dashboard; document vault beyond the verify page and library.
- Compliance map, bundles, team and accountant access.
- New document clusters beyond the launch set, industry packs, remaining Consumer & Civil Court documents (unlawful detainer, debt collection, bankruptcy).
- Verifier runs on non-launch documents (after launch, ordered by traffic).
- Admin console, public API, integrations, mobile app, Spanish.
- Any state other than California (schema is ready; content is not).
- IP protection and anti-scraping work (the search-first catalog in Part 8 is the MVP-level mitigation).
- Incentivized review programs of any kind.
- ML/AI-driven recommendations, behavioral personalization beyond explicitly entered events, lookalike suggestions.
- Team/shared templates, template marketplace, per-industry template packs.
- In-product commenting or collaboration on drafts.
- Tone levels beyond the approved launch set, per-paragraph tone mixing.
- Recipient-facing verify page blocks, "check a document you received" pages, and counterparty attribution (exports already show clause sourcing inline — revisit only if the data says recipients are a real channel).
- Push notifications.
- Freshness warranty / staleness refund promise (rejected by owner — revisit only when verifier coverage data supports the risk).
- Public law-change tracker page, independent methodology audit, report-a-stale-clause (post-launch trust multipliers).
- Anything requiring inference about the user's legal situation — permanently out of scope, not just deferred.

## DEFINITION OF DONE

- Every launch-set authority clause has a recorded adversarial result, with zero open blockers or majors.
- Honest verification levels and new tier definitions are live in the UI, tiering, validation, and methodology.
- A user can complete the interview free, see sources beside every clause, then buy and download a stamped document, with entitlement enforced server-side.
- Every filed document ships with a sourced filing instruction sheet; every fee and URL in it carries a check date.
- The verify page and trust page are live, generated from real data, and pass their privacy and consistency checks.
- A buyer has a persistent reason to return: named drafts sync, templates re-render from live law, the dashboard shows upcoming dates and honest suggestions.
- Every suggestion and prediction traces to a reviewed relation or a sourced date rule; nothing is AI-inferred; unreviewed relations cannot render.
- Tone changes wording style only through verified pre-authored variants; authority clauses never vary; exports and verify pages stay 1:1 truthful per variant.
- Templates contain zero legal text; drift detection covers saved documents, drafts, and template output.
- The subscription delivers: law-change watch (free for purchased, subscriber for everything), deadline calendar, annual "what changed" report, monthly document credit, unlimited subscriber edits/re-exports and e-signatures, and one-click document updates with diffs — all server-enforced and bypass-tested. The business setup roadmap is free and live.
- Catalog is search-first: no route, API, or sitemap enumerates the full corpus; only marketed documents are indexed; discovery beyond that happens through the reviewed relation map.
- Pull-back loops are live and capped: drift alerts, lifecycle digest, idle-draft reminders, and post-purchase sequence never exceed 1 email per user per week; unsubscribe kills all non-transactional mail.
- UPL shield complete: lint gates cover all advisory categories on every surface; tone is framed as style only; a test proves suggestions are non-individualized; interviews never steer; the canonical disclaimer is byte-identical everywhere; the guarantee covers product quality only; defense records are append-only and inventoried; RUNBOOK_UPL.md exists.
- No lawyer involvement anywhere in the product or plan (owner decision); the accepted risk is logged in DECISIONS.md.
- The registered agent referral link renders with disclosure and leaks no user data; the day-7 review request email works.
- The 30-day money-back guarantee is live in copy and enforced by the refund flow.
- Read-a-contract works free with no accuracy regression.
- All test-mode payment flows pass; live mode is switched on only by me.
- Account deletion removes all retention data; analytics carry no user content.
- Retention metrics (draft return rate, template reuse rate, suggestion conversion, digest engagement, update-application rate) are collecting and reportable weekly.
- Legal pages, refund and renewal copy are owner-finalized.
- Staging, backups, monitoring, and alerts are live.
- Wave 1 (the single-member LLC wedge) is published, the user test has run, the pilot plan is written with go/no-go criteria, and analytics are collecting.
- LAUNCH_READINESS.md shows all pass, or accepted risks recorded.
